documents.title: ISBI International Society for Burn Injuries practice guidelines for burn care

chunks.content: Introduction Cervical scar contracture is a common complication following burn injuries in the neck region. In addition to causing cosmetic deformities, severe cervical scar contracture often leads to functional impairments, such as incomplete mouth closure and limited neck mobility, which can significantly impact the patient’s physical and psychological well-being [ ]. In pediatric patients, the consequences of scar contracture may progressively worsen as the child grows, further compromising function. Currently, for cervical scar contractures that impair function, surgical treatments such as Z-plasty or flap reconstruction are commonly recommended [ – ]. However, in addition to the invasive nature of surgery and the airway risks associated with cervical procedures, postoperative complications such as flap necrosis, poor wound healing, and recurrence of contracture occur at a relatively high incidence. Therefore, finding effective non-surgical treatment alternatives is of significant importance [ ]. Since 2013, the Department of Burn and Plastic Surgery at our hospital has developed a Custom-Made Cervical Orthosis specifically tailored for pediatric patients with cervical scar contracture. Clinical applications have shown promising results, with this orthosis offering a viable alternative to surgical interventions in certain cases. The present study introduces the treatment method using custom-made cervical orthoses and analyzes its efficacy in a series of cases. Materials and methods Patients The present study utilized a self-controlled design. Due to ethical considerations, no parallel control group was established. A total of 11 pediatric patients admitted to the Department of Burns and Plastic Surgery at Quhua Hospital of Zhejiang from June 2019 to June 2024 were included in this study and underwent treatment with a Custom-Made Cervical Orthosis. The specific inclusion criteria were as follows: Age < 18 years; Presence of severe cervical scar contractures secondary to burn injury; No prior surgical treatment to the neck, including skin grafting or scar revision; Received custom-made cervical orthosis therapy > 6 months. Preparation of the cervical orthosis and treatment method The preparation of the cervical orthosis followed these steps: First, the patient’s neck circumference and neck length were measured. Cotton pads were then cut to appropriate sizes based on these measurements. Typically, the length of the cotton pad was about 5 cm shorter than the patient’s neck circumference, while the thickness of the pad was adjusted according to the neck length. The cotton pad was rolled tightly in a towel-like manner and then wrapped diagonally with large gauze (Fig. a). During treatment with the custom-made cervical orthosis, the patient was positioned in a seated posture with the head tilted backward or lying flat with the head tilted backward. The prepared neck brace was then placed around the neck and gently tightened by the patient’s hands to ensure a snug fit. A knot was tied at the back of the neck, with the tension adjusted so that one finger could fit comfortably between the orthosis and the neck, ensuring the patient could tolerate it. The chin was typically kept parallel to the ground or slightly elevated, and the orthosis should not extend beyond the chin to prevent excessive looseness, which would undermine the effectiveness of the pressure (Fig. b). Typically, when the patient’s neck scar is in the proliferative phase, the cervical orthosis needs to be worn continuously for 24 h a day. While during the scar atrophic phase, it can be adjusted to be worn during the day, with relaxation at night. Its size and tightness should be continuously adjusted based on changes in the patient’s neck extension. Other rehabilitation measures In addition to the custom-made cervical orthosis, all patients received a comprehensive and standardized rehabilitation program. Topical anti-scar medications were routinely applied to the cervical region, including silicone gel (Scar-ban) or compound heparin sodium and allantoin gel (Contractubex) [ , ]. Based on specific clinical indications and the preferences of the patients or their legal guardians, a subset of patients also underwent fractional laser therapy targeted at the cervical scars. Considering the significant risks of systemic side effects in the pediatric population—most notably the suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and potential growth retardation, as well as local complications like skin atrophy—none of the patients received intralesional corticosteroid injections [ ]. Furthermore, for burn injuries involving other anatomical sites, general rehabilitation interventions were implemented. These measures included the application of topical medications, pressure therapy, functional stretching exercises, and Activities of Daily Living (ADL)-oriented functional training, aiming to prevent further scar contracture and facilitate the overall functional recovery of the patients post-injury [ ]. Data collection Patient demographic data and injury details were collected. To evaluate the therapeutic efficacy of the custom-made cervical orthosis, measurements of the cervicomental angle (CMA) and cervical range of motion (ROM) were performed before and after treatment. Data collection Patient demographic data and injury details were collected. To evaluate the therapeutic efficacy of the custom-made cervical orthosis, measurements of the cervicomental angle (CMA) and cervical range of motion (ROM) were performed before and after treatment. To ensure maximal consistency, all clinical measurements were performed by the same senior rehabilitation physician. For each parameter, three consecutive measurements were taken using a standard goniometer and clinical photography, with the average value recorded for analysis to minimize random measurement error. The physician followed standardized anatomical landmarks for all assessments to ensure longitudinal reproducibility. CMA was defined as the angle formed by the line connecting the mandibular angle to the hyoid bone and the line from the hyoid bone to the suprasternal notch (upper border of the sternum) [ ]. Cervical ROM covered five specific directions—extension, left lateral flexion, right lateral flexion, left rotation, and right rotation. For extension measurement, the goniometer axis was placed over the external auditory meatus with the stationary arm perpendicular to the floor and the moving arm aligned with the base of the nares; for lateral flexion, the axis was placed over the C7 spinous process with the stationary arm kept vertical to prevent shoulder compensation and the moving arm aligned with the external occipital protuberance; and for rotation, the examiner took a superior view from the cranial vertex, placing the axis over the center of the vertex while the stationary arm was held parallel to the bi-acromial line and the moving arm was aligned with the tip of the nose [ , ]. The clinical symptoms related to cervical contracture caused by the patients before and after the treatment were also recorded. At discharge, patient satisfaction was assessed via the 24-item Inpatient Satisfaction Questionnaire (IPSQ). Items were rated from 1 (very dissatisfied) to 5 (very satisfied), yielding a total score out of 120 [ , ]. Additionally, during the final follow-up, the long-term quality of cervical scars was evaluated using the Patient and Observer Scar Assessment Scale (POSAS), which consists of two parts: the Observer Scar Assessment Scale (OSAS) and the Patient Scar Assessment Scale (PSAS). Under this assessment framework, the patient and a trained observer independently scored various parameters of the scar, including itching, pain, color, stiffness, thickness, and regularity, with lower scores indicating scar conditions closer to normal skin [ ]. Detailed contents of the IPSQ and POSAS scales are provided in Appendix 1. Statistical analysis The normality of the data was tested using the Shapiro-Wilk test. For normally distributed data, values were expressed as mean ± SD, and significant differences before and after treatment were assessed using paired t-tests. For non-normally distributed continuous variables, data were expressed as median (25th percentile − 75th percentile), and significant differences were evaluated using paired samples Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Categorical variables were expressed as number (percentage) and compared using the Fisher exact test. To further quantify the clinical magnitude of therapeutic efficacy, both percentage change and effect sizes were calculated. The percentage change for continuous variables was derived based on the group means using the formula: [(Mean post - Mean pre ) /Mean pre ]×100%. To ensure robust estimation given the small sample size, 95% confidence intervals (CI) for the percentage change were generated using a bootstrapping method with 10,000 resamples. Effect sizes were determined using Cohen’s d for paired samples (d z ), defined as the mean difference divided by the standard deviation of the difference. Effect sizes were interpreted according to Cohen’s conventional guidelines: 0.2 (small), 0.5 (medium), and 0.8 (large) [ ]. For categorical clinical symptoms, percentage change was calculated as the relative reduction in incidence. Additionally, to evaluate potential confounding effects, a subgroup analysis was conducted to compare improvement magnitudes and assessment scores between patients who received adjunctive fractional laser therapy and those who did not. Group comparisons were performed using the independent samples t-test for normally distributed variables and the Mann-Whitney U test for non-normally distributed variables. A p-value of < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. All statistical analyses were performed using R software version 4.2.2. Results Demographic and clinical characteristics of the pediatric patients Among the 11 pediatric patients who underwent treatment with the custom-made cervical orthosis, 8 (72.7%) were male and 3 (27.3%) were female. The median age of all patients was 2 (interquartile range [IQR], 1–3) years. The mean total body surface area (TBSA) affected by burns was 16 ± 11% TBSA, while the median area of third-degree burns was 4 (IQR, 2–8) % TBSA. The cervical burn wounds of all patients healed via secondary intention (spontaneous healing). At a median of 1 (IQR, 0–3) month following wound healing, patients initiated treatment with the custom-made cervical orthosis and continued for more than six months, with a mean treatment duration of 13 ± 5 (range 6–24) months. Regarding adjunctive therapies, all patients utilized standard topical medications, including Silicone Gel (Scar-ban, n = 10) or Compound Heparin Sodium and Allantoin Gel (Contractubex, n = 1), and 4 patients (36.4%) received between 1 and 4 sessions of fractional laser therapy during their follow-up, while the remaining 7 (63.6%) patients did not receive any fractional laser therapy to the neck (Table ). Appendix 2 further documents detailed individual baseline characteristics and treatment specifics. Data are shown as the median (25th percentile, 75th percentile), mean±standard deviation or the number of patients (%), as appropriate. Time Post-injury: Duration from the initial burn injury to the start of orthosis treatment; Time Post-healing: Duration from wound closure to the start of orthosis treatment. Comparison of cervical scar contracture before and after custom-made cervical orthosis Neck scar contracture-related variables before and after treatment are summarized in Table ; Fig. . Following treatment, the CMA significantly decreased from a median of 140° (IQR: 130°–155°) before treatment to 120° (IQR: 115°–120°) after treatment ( p < 0.001), representing a 16.6% reduction (95% CI: -20.5% to -12.2%) with a large effect size (Cohen’s d = 1.84, 95% CI: 0.87 to 2.81). The cervical ROM showed significant improvements in all five directions ( p < 0.001). Notably, cervical extension increased by 183.7% (95% CI: 119.0% to 317.2%; Cohen’s d = 3.92, 95% CI: 2.18 to 5.66), and rotation improved by over 165%. Additionally, the incidence of clinical symptoms associated with cervical scar contracture decreased significantly after treatment. All patients exhibited complete resolution of inability to close the mouth, facial organ displacement and forced head flexion. The prevalence of lower lip eversion was reduced to only one patient after treatment. Patient satisfaction and scar follow-up results The evaluation of treatment satisfaction at discharge resulted in a mean IPSQ score of 106.55 ± 5.92, indicating high guardian satisfaction with the custom-made cervical orthosis. All patients completed a follow-up period of more than two years without any surgical intervention for the neck. At the final follow-up, the median POSAS score for long-term scar quality was 19 (IQR: 14–21), suggesting that the cervical scars had achieved satisfactory aesthetic and functional maturation. Subgroup analysis of adjunctive fractional laser therapy To evaluate the potential confounding effect of adjunctive CO2 fractional laser therapy, a subgroup analysis was performed comparing patients who received laser treatment ( n = 4) with those who did not ( n = 7). The results are summarized in Table . There were no significant differences between the two subgroups in the improvement of CMA ( p = 0.285) or in most cervical ROM parameters, including lateral flexion and rotation (all p > 0.05). Notably, the laser group demonstrated a significantly greater improvement in cervical extension compared to the non-laser group (median: 45.0° [IQR, 43.8–46.2] vs. 30.0° [IQR, 27.5–35.0], p = 0.013; Cohen’s d = 2.39, 95%CI 0.81 to 3.97). Regarding patient-reported and clinical assessments, no significant differences were observed between the subgroups in either the IPSQ scores at discharge ( p = 0.152) or the POSAS scores at the final follow-up ( p = 1.000). Case presentation Case 1 involves a 1-year-old male infant who sustained scald burns covering 15% TBSA, involving the face, neck, anterior chest, and extremities. Hypertrophic scarring developed in the cervical region during the healing process. Complete wound healing was achieved approximately two months post-injury, and the patient was admitted to our hospital three months later due to severe scar contracture and associated deformities. Pre-treatment assessment revealed significant restriction in the cervical ROM: flexion 30°, extension 0°, left lateral flexion 10°, right lateral flexion 10°, left rotation 10°, and right rotation 10°. Clinically, the patient presented with lower lip eversion, incompetence of oral closure, displacement of facial features, and a forward head posture. Following admission, the patient underwent an 8-month course of treatment with a custom-made cervical orthosis. hospital three months later due to severe scar contracture and associated deformities. Pre-treatment assessment revealed significant restriction in the cervical ROM: flexion 30°, extension 0°, left lateral flexion 10°, right lateral flexion 10°, left rotation 10°, and right rotation 10°. Clinically, the patient presented with lower lip eversion, incompetence of oral closure, displacement of facial features, and a forward head posture. Following admission, the patient underwent an 8-month course of treatment with a custom-made cervical orthosis. Adjunctive therapies included the daily application of topical silicone gel (Scar-ban) and three sessions of fractional laser therapy (at approximately 1, 3, and 5 months post-admission). After 8 months of intervention, the hypertrophic scarring was markedly reduced. Cervical ROM improved significantly to: flexion 50°, extension 45°, left lateral flexion 45°, right lateral flexion 40°, left rotation 65°, and right rotation 60°. The CMA decreased from 175° to 135°, and all pre-existing clinical symptoms were effectively resolved. At the 2-year post-treatment follow-up, the patient exhibited no significant clinical symptoms in the cervical region, and the remaining scars did not interfere with his ADL. The follow-up POSAS score for the neck was 34, and the IPSQ score was 110. The treatment timeline and representative clinical photographs are presented in Fig. . Case 2 involves a 3-year-old male patient who sustained alcohol flame burns covering 42% TBSA, involving the head, face, neck, trunk, and upper extremities, with 25% TBSA being III-Degree burns. Wounds achieved complete healing approximately two months post-injury, and the patient was admitted to our center for rehabilitation one month later. At admission, the patient exhibited significant hypertrophic scarring in the cervical region with a baseline CMA of 150°. Pre-treatment cervical ROM was: flexion 50°, extension 40°, left lateral flexion 45°, right lateral flexion 45°, left rotation 60°, and right rotation 60°. Clinical presentation included lower lip ectropion, incompetence of oral closure, and a forced forward-flexed head posture.Treatment for the cervical region consisted of a custom-made cervical orthosis and daily application of topical silicone gel (Scar-ban); notably, no fractional laser therapy was administered to the neck scars during the treatment period. For burn injuries at other anatomical sites, general rehabilitation interventions were implemented, including several sessions of fractional laser therapy on the face and chest. Following 24 months of continuous orthosis therapy, the CMA improved to 120°, and cervical ROM significantly increased to: flexion 50°, extension 60°, left lateral flexion 45°, right lateral flexion 45°, left rotation 80°, and right rotation 80°. Approximately one year into the treatment, the patient developed prominent keloids on the bilateral ears and left shoulder due to his keloid diathesis. These were subsequently managed via scar excision and suturing at an external facility (ears) and scar release at our hospital (upper limbs and left shoulder). At the 4-year follow-up, the cervical region—which had received no surgical intervention—showed stable scar maturation with no significant clinical symptoms or functional limitations in ADL. The follow-up cervical POSAS score was 21, and the IPSQ score was 108. The treatment timeline and representative clinical photographs are presented in Fig. . Discussion In recent years, as advancements in acute burn care have improved survival rates, the management of post-burn scar contractures has become a paramount challenge [ ]. Cervical contracture is one of the most common and severe sequelae, leading to impairments in movement, breathing, speech, and nutrition, as well as aesthetic disfigurement. This problem is particularly pronounced in pediatric patients, who face a unique set of physiological challenges distinct from adults [ ]. The primary contribution of this study is the demonstration that a non-invasive, custom-made orthosis can effectively manage severe contractures in this vulnerable demographic, filling a critical clinical gap for toddlers and young children for whom early surgical intervention carries high risks of recurrence and perioperative complications. Treating neck contractures in young children requires a fundamental departure from adult protocols, primarily due to the mechanism of “growth antagonism.” Unlike the static anatomy of adults, the pediatric cervical spine and mandible undergo rapid elongation. In the presence of rigid hypertrophic scarring, this somatic growth creates a dynamic tension where the skeletal frame lengthens while the pathological scar tissue remains static. This antagonism generates a continuous flexion moment that can progressively worsen the deformity, potentially leading to irreversible secondary skeletal complications such as micrognathia, dental malocclusion, and cervical kyphosis [ , ]. While surgical release is the standard for mature contractures, its application in growing children is often complicated by “growth-induced recurrence,” necessitating repeated procedures to keep pace with skeletal development [ , , ]. Our non-surgical orthotic approach offers a strategic advantage by managing these contractures dynamically during growth. By providing continuous mechanical counter-tension, this method potentially spares young children from the compounding physiological and psychological trauma of invasive procedures, including the potential systemic risks associated with repeated general anesthesia and surgical stress [

While surgical release is the standard for mature contractures, its application in growing children is often complicated by “growth-induced recurrence,” necessitating repeated procedures to keep pace with skeletal development [ , , ]. Our non-surgical orthotic approach offers a strategic advantage by managing these contractures dynamically during growth. By providing continuous mechanical counter-tension, this method potentially spares young children from the compounding physiological and psychological trauma of invasive procedures, including the potential systemic risks associated with repeated general anesthesia and surgical stress [ – ]. Ultimately, the early and consistent implementation of orthotic therapy allows for the optimization of functional outcomes while ensuring that the treatment remains in harmony with the child’s ongoing physical development. Continuous pressure therapy acts as a cornerstone in pediatric scar management, functioning through mechanotransduction to modulate the fibroproliferative response. By applying sustained mechanical loading, pressure devices create local hypoxia and downregulate mechanosensitive pathways, thereby inhibiting myofibroblast differentiation and promoting orderly collagen realignment [ , ]. This intervention is uniquely advantageous in children, whose active somatic growth and high collagen turnover rates endow their tissue with superior biological plasticity compared to adults. Consequently, early mechanical intervention can effectively steer the immature pediatric scar toward a normotrophic phenotype before irreversible fibrosis establishes [ – ]. The use of orthotic devices is one of the most effective methods for delivering continuous pressure therapy to cervical scars [ ]. However, it has been observed that conventional plastic orthoses are often too rigid, preventing a snug fit around the neck and offering inadequate pressure distribution; specifically, they fail to conform to the complex concave-convex curves of a child’s neck, leading to uneven pressure application. Some cervical braces, designed for general surgical use, employ soft inner foam for enhanced comfort; however, they fail to provide sufficient pressure to manage the contracture effectively [ ]. Our custom-made cervical orthosis was designed to overcome these limitations, offering several key advantages especially relevant to pediatric care. First, the snug fit of our orthosis ensures optimal pressure distribution via “stress shielding,” effectively converting the mechanical tension of growth into a remodeling force. Second, the design of the orthosis incorporates cotton padding and large gauze, which not only provides sufficient rigidity to maintain the functional position of the neck but also allows for slight movement, reducing tension caused by limited neck rotation. This dynamic conformity is critical for pediatric compliance, as it accommodates swallowing and spontaneous head rotation without generating the shear forces that cause pain in active toddlers. Third, the orthosis is easy to apply and replace, with a simple manufacturing process. Given the rapid somatic growth of children, this adjustability ensures the device can “grow with the child,” avoiding the frequent and costly replacements required by rigid custom molds. Fourth, because pediatric skin is thinner and more fragile, scars are prone to blistering and ulceration during recovery. The breathable cotton and gauze construction helps prevent maceration and infection by protecting the area. Additionally, the innermost layer of the orthosis can be used in combination with silicone gel sheets or other scar management products, further enhancing its effectiveness in preventing and treating scar formation. Collectively, these structural and functional refinements allow the device to overcome the pitfalls of conventional orthotic devices, offering a cost-effective and highly adaptable strategy tailored to the unique developmental demands of growing children. In this self-controlled case series, patients treated with the custom orthosis achieved significant improvements in both the CMA and cervical ROM. While direct comparisons with surgical literature must be approached with caution due to heterogeneity in patient age and scar maturity, our functional outcomes align with the improvements reported in surgical series [ , ]. For example, in a report by Geneviève et al. [ ], a total of nine patients, including children and adults, with cervical contracture were treated surgically. Preoperative average neck mobility in five directions (Extension, Left lateral flexion, Right lateral flexion, Left rotation, Right rotation) was 24°, 19°, 24°, 46°, and 40°, respectively; after free flap surgery, mobility improved to 47°, 34°, 33°, 66°, and 69°, respectively. In our series of 11 pediatric patients, the pre-treatment average neck mobility in the five directions was 20°, 24°, 24°, 28°, and 29°, respectively; post-treatment, it improved to 56°, 43°, 43°, 74°, and 74°, respectively. Zhang et al. [ ] highlighted the functional and aesthetic importance of the CMA and, through surgical treatment, successfully reshaped the CMA to 90–120° in 50 severe cervical burn contracture cases. In comparison, our non-surgical treatment reduced the CMA from a median of 140°to 120°. Crucially, our study observed a significant resolution of clinical symptoms, including the inability to close the mouth and facial distortion. [ ] highlighted the functional and aesthetic importance of the CMA and, through surgical treatment, successfully reshaped the CMA to 90–120° in 50 severe cervical burn contracture cases. In comparison, our non-surgical treatment reduced the CMA from a median of 140°to 120°. Crucially, our study observed a significant resolution of clinical symptoms, including the inability to close the mouth and facial distortion. These improvements are reflected in the high satisfaction scores reported by parents (IPSQ), as parents valued the ability to correct functional and aesthetic deformities while sparing their children from the risks of surgery. Furthermore, our long-term follow-up results showed a median POSAS score of 19 (IQR: 14–21), which is categorized as mild scar severity. This indicates that the neck scars of pediatric patients treated with custom-made orthoses have successfully matured with a minimal aesthetic burden [ , ]. Collectively, these findings highlight that our custom-made cervical orthoses serve as a cost-effective and high-compliance strategy, effectively leveraging physiological remodeling mechanisms to avoid the necessity of surgical intervention. Notably, in this study, a subset of patients received adjunctive CO2 fractional laser therapy, which warrants careful consideration. Our subgroup analysis revealed that while the laser group achieved a significantly greater improvement in cervical extension, no significant differences were observed in CMA correction, other ROM parameters, or treatment satisfaction (IPSQ) and scar maturation (POSAS) outcomes. These findings suggest that adjunctive laser therapy may act synergistically with the orthosis to achieve superior functional outcomes, likely by enhancing scar elasticity through collagen remodeling [ ]. However, it is crucial to emphasize that patients in the non-laser group also achieved substantial and clinically meaningful improvements across all functional and structural domains, including a median extension increase of 30.0°. This indicates that while multimodal management is beneficial, the custom-made cervical orthosis remains the fundamental driver of contracture resolution. Additionally, it is important to acknowledge that the observed improvements likely result from a synergistic effect of the orthosis intervention and the natural maturation process inherent to pediatric scars. As all patients in our study initiated treatment within 6 months post-injury—corresponding to the active proliferative phase of scar formation—the orthosis was uniquely positioned to guide this vigorous biological remodeling into a functional anatomical alignment. This mechanical guidance effectively counteracted the retractive forces of the maturing scar, preventing the contracture that would typically occur if the tissue were left to heal without direction. Drawing upon our clinical experience in managing pediatric patients with neck scar contracture, we proposed a clinical decision algorithm to guide therapeutic strategy selection (Fig. ). Beyond the quantitative clinical results, we share two typical cases that successfully regained cervical mobility and symptom relief through custom-made cervical orthosis, thereby avoiding the necessity of surgical intervention. These cases also highlight the value of multimodal management: Case 1 exemplifies the efficacy of combining orthoses with fractional CO 2 laser to expedite the softening of active scars [ ]. Case 2 reveals that even for patients with a keloid diathesis—manifested by keloids on the ears and shoulders—the continuous pressure provided by the orthosis remains a potent strategy for inhibiting cervical contracture [ ]. Several limitations of this study should be acknowledged. First and most critically, our results are constrained by the inherent limitations of a self-controlled case series design, which restricts causal inference. The absence of a concurrent comparator group—such as a cohort receiving standard pressure therapy alone or undergoing observation only—makes it difficult to definitively isolate the therapeutic efficacy of the orthosis from the natural maturation of pediatric hypertrophic scars. Given that such scars can undergo significant spontaneous remodeling over 24–36 months, the lack of a formal temporal control analysis makes it challenging to quantify the specific contribution of the orthotic intervention beyond this biological progression [ ]. Second, the small sample size ( n = 11) restricts the statistical power and the generalizability of our findings. Third, the potential for selection bias cannot be excluded, as successful long-term orthotic treatment depends heavily on high treatment compliance from both patients and their guardians, which may not fully represent the broader pediatric population with neck scar contractures. Fourth, although CMA and ROM measurements were standardized and performed by a single senior evaluator, the lack of inter-rater or intra-rater reliability analysis leaves a potential risk of measurement bias. However, the observed improvements in CMA and ROM in our cohort substantially exceeded the 5° to 10° error margin typically associated with clinical goniometry [ , ]. This suggest that the changes are more likely to represent clinically meaningful progress than simple measurement variability. Finally, patient- or caregiver-reported outcome measures, such as the POSAS, were not implemented at the early stages of the study,

Finally, patient- or caregiver-reported outcome measures, such as the POSAS, were not implemented at the early stages of the study, leading to a relatively one-dimensional assessment of initial scar severity. Future multi-center prospective studies with larger cohorts and extended follow-up are warranted to validate these findings and to evaluate the long-term efficacy of this therapy, as well as its synergistic effects with other interventions. Conclusion Custom-made cervical orthoses provide significant anatomical and functional benefits for pediatric patients with post-burn cervical scar contractures. This non-surgical treatment effectively reduces the CMA, enhances neck mobility, and alleviates related clinical symptoms. Furthermore, the therapy yields high patient satisfaction; long-term follow-up exceeding two years demonstrated that the scars maintained a “mild scar severity” level. These findings underscore the clinical potential of this therapy, which may obviate the need for subsequent reconstructive surgery in a substantial proportion of pediatric patients.
